title: Permissions: GRANT, REVOKE, DENY
description: Control access to SQL Server securables using GRANT, REVOKE, and DENY at both server and database levels.

blocks.text: SQL Server permissions are granted to principals on securables. A securable can be a server, database, schema, table, view, stored procedure, or any other protected resource. Permissions can be granted, revoked, or denied. Understanding how these three operations interact is critical because DENY overrides GRANT and REVOKE removes a grant but does not block access.

blocks.title: DENY Overrides GRANT
blocks.text: If a user belongs to two roles and one role is granted SELECT while another is denied SELECT, the DENY wins. This is the most common source of unexpected permission failures in SQL Server.

Permissions are granular. SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE apply to tables and views. EXECUTE applies to stored procedures. CONTROL, ALTER, TAKE OWNERSHIP, and VIEW DEFINITION apply at the schema, database, or server level. The finer the permission, the more precisely you can enforce least privilege.

rows: See object metadata without data access

blocks.text: GRANT gives a principal a specific permission on a securable. When you GRANT a permission, the principal can perform that action unless a DENY overrides it. You can optionally grant the WITH GRANT OPTION, allowing the grantee to further grant the same permission to others.

blocks.title: Grant Database and Schema Permissions
blocks.content: Grant granular permissions at the database and schema level.

blocks.text: REVOKE removes a previously granted permission. It does not deny the permission; it simply removes the grant. If a DENY exists, REVOKE alone will not restore access. To fully restore access, you must REVOKE the DENY and then GRANT the permission again.

blocks.title: Revoke and Re-Grant Permissions
blocks.content: Remove a grant and restore access cleanly.

blocks.text: DENY explicitly blocks a permission. A DENY persists even if the principal is later added to a role that has the same permission granted. DENY is rarely needed in well-designed role-based systems, but it can be useful to explicitly block specific sensitive operations like disabling a constraint or dropping a table.

blocks.title: Deny Sensitive Operations
blocks.content: Explicitly deny dangerous operations to a role.

blocks.title: Effective Permissions
blocks.text: SQL Server computes effective permissions by evaluating all direct grants, role memberships, and DENY entries. Use fn_my_permissions to inspect what a specific principal can actually do in a given context.

blocks.title: Inspect Effective Permissions
blocks.content: Use the built-in function to see what a principal can do.

items.text: Grant permissions to roles, never directly to individual users
Avoid DENY in most permission designs
Document permission rationales in change control

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: GRANT gives access, REVOKE removes a grant, and DENY explicitly blocks access.
DENY always overrides GRANT, even across role memberships.
Permissions cascade from server to database to schema to object.
Use roles for all normal permission assignments and audit effective permissions regularly.
blocks.takeaway: Grant to roles, avoid DENY, and always verify effective permissions after changes.
